name: Chemistry
intro: Explore how particles explain materials, medicines and a changing planet. The BGE projects below are suggested S1–S3 experiences for departmental review. Senior Phase headings describe national courses; the activities are original practice, not assessed coursework. Carry out experiments only when directed by your teacher using school safety procedures.

bge.title: Kitchen chemistry
bge.question: Why does food change when it cooks?
learn: Use particle ideas to describe dissolving.
bge.task: Annotate three changes in a teacher-provided cooking video. Explain which evidence suggests a new substance formed.
bge.extend: Explain why melting chocolate is different from burning toast.

bge.title: Materials for a better world
bge.question: What makes a material suitable?
bge.task: Design packaging for a fragile object. Compare two materials using strength, mass and end-of-life evidence.
bge.extend: Challenge the claim that every biodegradable material is automatically sustainable.

bge.title: Acids and alkalis
bge.question: How can we describe acidity?
bge.task: Use a teacher-selected simulation to arrange five solutions by pH and predict changes when acid is neutralised.
bge.extend: Explain why pH alone does not tell you every hazard.

bge.title: Chemistry and our environment
bge.question: How can chemistry reduce pollution?
bge.task: Compare two published fuel data tables. Write a recommendation with a benefit, limitation and supporting figure.
bge.extend: Research how green hydrogen is produced and identify the source of its energy.

senior.title: Chemistry
senior.explain: Build chemical knowledge through practical enquiry. National 4 also includes an added-value assignment. Availability depends on school provision.
senior.assessment: Internally assessed units; National 4 includes added value. These courses are pass/fail.

senior.title: National 5 Chemistry
senior.explain: Study bonding, reaction rates, quantitative chemistry, carbon compounds, energy, metals and the chemical industry within the specification.
senior.assessment: Question paper and assignment under the current national assessment requirements. Practise independently; complete assessed work under teacher conditions.

senior.title: Higher Chemistry
senior.explain: Deepen understanding of periodicity, bonding, organic chemistry, equilibria, energy and chemical analysis. Researching Chemistry develops enquiry skills across content.
senior.assessment: Question paper and assignment; consult the current specification and teacher guidance for this session.

skills.title: Plan a fair comparison
skills.explain: Change one independent variable and measure a clearly defined outcome. Control other influential variables.
skills.try: Plan a simulation comparing reaction rate at three temperatures, with repeats.
skills.check: Have you stated what stays constant and how rate will be calculated?

skills.title: Write chemical equations
skills.explain: A balanced equation conserves the number of atoms of each element.
skills.try: Balance Mg + O₂ → MgO using coefficients only.
skills.check: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Never change formula subscripts to balance.

skills.title: Read graphs critically
skills.explain: A steeper product–time gradient indicates a faster rate at that moment.
skills.try: Sketch two product–time curves with the same final product but different initial rates.
skills.check: The faster curve levels off sooner at the same final height.

skills.title: Calculate with units
skills.explain: State the relationship, substitute values and carry units through the calculation.
skills.try: Calculate concentration when 0.20 mol solute makes 0.50 L solution.
skills.check: c = n/V = 0.40 mol L⁻¹; distinguish volume of solution from volume of solvent.

practice.question: A reaction produces 24 cm³ gas in 30 s. Calculate its average rate and explain one limitation of this average.
practice.hint: Divide change in volume by time; consider whether rate stays constant.
practice.answer: 24 ÷ 30 = 0.80 cm³ s⁻¹. This averages the whole interval and can hide a rapid start followed by slowing. State both the value and unit.
practice.extend: Explain how an initial-rate estimate could be obtained from a graph.

practice.question: Why does powdered calcium carbonate usually react faster than equal-mass large chips under otherwise identical conditions?
practice.hint: Think about exposed particles, not a change in chemical identity.
practice.answer: Powder has a greater surface area exposed to acid, allowing more successful collisions per second. It is not because the particles inside each grain have become smaller atoms.
practice.extend: Predict whether the final gas volume changes if the same limiting amount reacts completely.

practice.question: A claim says a fuel is carbon neutral because plants absorb CO₂. What evidence would you request?
practice.hint: Look beyond the moment of combustion.
practice.answer: Request lifecycle evidence for cultivation, fertiliser, processing, transport, land-use change and regrowth. Uptake alone does not establish a zero net impact.
practice.extend: Compare the boundaries used in two lifecycle studies.

resources.title: Royal Society of Chemistry Education
resources.task: Choose a sustainability article. Record one chemical explanation and one evidence-based question.

resources.title: PhET interactive simulations
resources.task: Find Balancing Chemical Equations. Explain why changing coefficients preserves substances.

resources.title: Royal Institution science films
resources.task: Choose a chemistry film and pause to predict an outcome. Do not recreate demonstrations at home.

resources.title: Qualifications Scotland past papers
resources.task: Select your level and compare an attempted chemistry answer with its marking instructions.

resources.title: Understanding Standards
resources.task: Find Chemistry and discuss why evidence earns credit. Some materials are restricted to staff.

ipad.title: Particle explanation
steps: Draw a labelled before-and-after particle model.
Record a 40-second explanation of what changes.
Add captions distinguishing particles from substances.
ipad.evidence: An annotated explanation, not a photograph without reasoning.

ipad.title: Data storyteller
steps: Enter a teacher-provided dataset in Numbers.
Create a labelled scatter graph with appropriate units.
Annotate the trend and one anomalous result.
ipad.evidence: A graph plus an evidence-based conclusion.

ipad.title: Retrieval cards
steps: Create six question cards after a lesson.
Record your explanation before checking notes.
Correct one misconception in a different colour.
ipad.evidence: A dated set showing how your explanation improved.

careers.title: Laboratory technician
careers.linkToLearning: Accurate measurement, records and safety support reliable testing.
careers.nextStep: Explore college science routes and laboratory apprenticeships on My World of Work.

careers.title: Chemical engineer
careers.linkToLearning: Reaction rates and energy connect to efficient industrial processes.
careers.nextStep: Compare accredited university chemical engineering entry requirements.

careers.title: Environmental analyst
careers.linkToLearning: Chemical evidence informs water quality and pollution decisions.
careers.nextStep: Investigate college environmental science and university chemistry pathways.

careers.title: Pharmacy and pharmaceutical science
careers.linkToLearning: Structures, concentration and quality assurance support medicines work.
careers.nextStep: Compare pharmacist degree routes with pharmacy support and technician training.

parentTip: Ask your young person to explain one everyday change using particles. Encourage a clear explanation and a question for class; avoid trying chemical demonstrations at home.

visual.title: Count atoms, not just symbols
visual.question: The equation is 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Count each type of atom on both sides. Why must the small formula numbers stay unchanged?
visual.answer: Both sides contain 4 hydrogen atoms and 2 oxygen atoms. Coefficients change the amount of each substance; changing a formula subscript changes the substance.
